idiom_name: abstract base class with protected provided operations and an abstract sandbox method
implementation_notes: TypeScript spells the pattern in the compiler's vocabulary: abstract classes cannot be instantiated, abstract members must be implemented by the subclass, and protected members are reachable from derived classes but not from clients - the handbook's classes chapter documents both modifiers and the rule that a derived class may widen a protected member to public. The wall is compile-time only: the modifiers are erased, so any JavaScript consumer (or an as-cast) can still call a primitive, and #private fields cannot serve as the primitive API at all because subclasses cannot see them. Where the behaviours share no state, a Sandbox interface - the engine operations plus the state they need - handed to a function or a class is the lighter idiom, since structural typing requires no hierarchy. Keep the abstract-class form when the family shares instance state and a registration lifecycle, and pair it with override so a renamed primitive fails the build.
pitfalls: protected is erased at run time: a plain JavaScript caller, a decorator or an as-cast can invoke a primitive, and a subclass may widen a primitive to public on override, so the sandbox is a compile-time contract rather than a runtime one.

Field initialisation order bites exactly here - a base-class constructor that calls the sandbox method runs before the subclass's field initialisers, and with useDefineForClassFields the fields are not merely undefined but explicitly defined later.

The same member marked protected in a class makes structural assignment stricter than it looks: objects that appear to have the right shape are rejected unless they come from the hierarchy, which surprises authors who expect duck typing.
Because everything is erased, tests can only rely on the compiler: a missing override of a protected member is caught, but a runtime path that bypasses the sandbox is not.
